articles.headline: How did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?
keyFacts: Democrats won major midterm victories in North Carolina, flipping a US Senate seat, five House seats, and the statehouse.
Democratic and Republican party officials attributed the losses to Republican complacency, weak turnout efforts, and unfulfilled campaign promises.
As of Monday, four House races remained uncalled, while North Carolina's state senate margin is headed to a recount.
body: Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the country in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as North Carolina.

Democrats flipped a US Senate seat for the first time since 2008, as well as five House seats, one of which Cook Political Report had rated “solid” Republican, and four others considered “likely” Republican. Democrats also held power in the state’s first district, which Republicans had targeted in a redistricting effort.

One of the seats Democrats flipped belonged to Richard Hudson, a representative who led House Republicans’ re-election efforts as the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. It was the first time an NRCC chair had ever lost a general election.
As of Monday, the Associated Press hadn’t called four of the House races, but two were leaning in favor of Democrats.

North Carolina’s statehouse flipped for Democrats for the first time in more than a decade and Republicans are holding onto the state senate by a one-seat margin – which is currently headed to a recount.

This was all in a state that had only voted for one Democratic presidential candidate since 1980, and hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost 20 years. So how did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?
“They took voters for granted,” said Anderson Clayton, the 28-year-old chair of the North Carolina Democratic party.

“They thought they could gerrymander themselves into having a seat and not actually have to go out and fight for it, and I think voters looked at them and said: ‘That’s not how we roll. That’s not how it works in North Carolina.’”

Clayton, who has been working to flip North Carolina blue since she was elected in 2023, points to multiple factors this election cycle: Trump’s unpopularity fueling North Carolinians’ frustrations with the current status quo, and a fleet of younger candidates running for office.
But she emphasized Republicans’ failure to address issues affecting voters, especially in North Carolina’s rural districts, as one of the top reasons.
As an example, she pointed to a recent quote from Donny Lambeth, a seven-term Republican state representative, who lost by eight percentage points.

Lambeth told the New York Times that he mistakenly listened to members of his caucus who told him he was in a “safe district” and did not need to spend “any money”. In 2024, Lambeth had won by approximately 14 percentage points.
“I was like: ‘Well, did you go out and talk to any of your voters?’” Clayton said in response to Lambeth’s admission. “‘Like, did you actually speak to somebody on the ground in your district?’”
Felice Pete, an RNC committee member from North Carolina and longtime Republican activist, acknowledged Republicans’ shortcomings.

“You have places where we didn’t think we’re going to lose, like Virginia Foxx, and looking back, people took it for granted. These were safe, red counties. And it’s just getting out the vote effort,” Pete said.

The Associated Press has not called Foxx’s race in North Carolina’s fifth congressional district because of an ongoing recount, but her Democratic opponent, Chuck Hubbard, is ahead by a thin but likely insurmountable margin.

“The 2024 win for Republicans was not done with traditional Republicans,” Pete said. “They were first-time voters, they were independents, there were a lot of young minority men, a lot of young college-aged men.”
“I just think, with redistricting, we just did not have the effort focused with getting out the votes,” Pete said.

Republicans had invested time, money and energy into maintaining their majority through redistricting, under pressure from the US president. They redrew lines to try to flip the first congressional district, but it didn’t work; the incumbent Democrat, Don Davis, held onto his seat.
Clayton accused Republicans of getting “elitist” in the midterms and relying too heavily on consultants – a criticism Democrats often face.
“Instead, you had real grassroots energy from Democrats that won seats that honestly, they shouldn’t have, in some ways, on Tuesday night,” Clayton said.

In parts of the state that are comfortably red, such as Davidson county, located in central North Carolina, the electorate moved 16 percentage points in favor of Democrats compared with 2024, according to NBC’s decision desk.
Christopher Jessup, the chair of the Davidson county Republican party and a longtime Republican advocate, said he wasn’t sure why that happened but attributed it to “probably some voter turnout”.

Jessup highlighted that his county still overwhelmingly voted for the Republican candidates in the midterms, and praised the work his colleagues and teams did. Despite that, the sixth congressional district, where Davidson county is located, flipped for Democrats.
When asked what the top issue for voters in the county was, Jessup said “a very negative view of Roy Cooper”.
Cooper, the former governor of North Carolina, defeated Michael Whatley, the former head of the Republican National Committee and chosen directly by Trump, by nearly 20 percentage points.
Republicans had anticipated Cooper’s win. By October, the top Super Pac for Senate Republicans cancelled remaining ads that it had booked in the state.

Like many Republicans, Pete is still dissecting why messaging that won over North Carolinians in 2024 didn’t resonate in 2026. But she has some theories, starting with the fact that Trump 2024 voters felt “betrayed”.

“The word that I hear over and over is betrayal,” Pete said. “Many of those people felt like voting did not matter because they felt like 2024 was their last hope to have this correction, and then they go, and here we are.”

Pete pointed to Trump’s campaign promise not to start more wars, which he failed to deliver on when he started a conflict with Iran in February. That conflict, which Congress never formally approved, has pushed gas and diesel prices up, causing a chain reaction that has affected other everyday costs, such as groceries.

She added that messaging that won voters over in 2024 “started to shift” or wasn’t being communicated well from “some higher-ups, or even our administration”. That includes mass deportations; during his campaign, Trump promised to target every undocumented immigrant, but administration officials now claim they target undocumented immigrants with violent criminal histories.

Citing a personal example, Pete said the young men that she gathered to go out door-knocking in 2024 did not want to work for the 2026 midterms; she called the experience “a microcosm of what happened”.
“We have to have an honest assessment of that and just the detriment of not fulfilling, or seemingly fulfilling, the promises you make,” Pete said.

articles.headline: Can a TV be too large? An investigation
keyFacts: A TechCrunch writer upgraded their home television to a 65-inch LG evo C4 OLED screen.
The writer experienced temporary nausea and headaches, which other online users also reported after adopting large OLED displays.
The writer's symptoms ended after a few days once their eyes adjusted to the display's size.
body: For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.

The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows.
In short: They look way better.

They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024.

At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic.

However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache.
In short: Not great.

I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain.

“I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.”

Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?”

There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen.

Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having.

In considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a big screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car.

After a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison.

Initial physiological reactions aside, the size of the 65-inch screen (and whether your living space actually has room for it) is still something that needs to be considered carefully by potential buyers. I recently moved into a place with a slightly bigger living room, which has given me the flexibility to install a bigger device. At my old apartment, however, this size of TV would have definitely felt like it was devouring the space.

Another slight frustration is that the C4 does not come with any detailed installation instructions. The screen (which is so wide it’s difficult to move without another person there to help you) comes detached from its base, and the user is just sort of expected to figure out how to effectively move and put together the two pieces. A quick YouTube video is all that is necessary to understand this process, but you have to be careful when moving and assembling the pieces so as not to scratch or damage the screen.

Once the whole thing is set up and assembled, the OLED is a truly beautiful thing to behold. The customization that’s possible, including advanced brightness and color control — and things like “Filmmaker Mode” (which claims to adjust each movie’s color and frame rate settings to those intended by the director) — make the user experience really powerful.

To sum up: The evo C4 is a really spectacular piece of equipment that has a lot to offer the avid home entertainment viewer — although there may be a bit of a learning curve before it makes your cinema dreams come true.

articles.headline: You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?
keyFacts: A reader asked Vox for advice after her non-religious husband developed severe sleep-disrupting anxiety about AI-driven human extinction.
The columnist stated that religious traditions offer moral frameworks and stories that can help people navigate technological uncertainty.
The columnist recommended encouraging the husband if he finds a religious community that promotes agency rather than despair.
body: Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form . Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity:

My husband and I are not religious. He’s from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and I grew up attending an interdenominational church, but we don’t attend services now. Lately, though, he’s become so anxious about AI safety and the possibility of human extinction that he’s been having trouble sleeping. In the wake of all this existential uncertainty, he’s expressed a renewed interest in attending church. And he’s not interested in the UU church (with its believe-what-you-want attitude); he said he needs “the strong stuff.”

It’s all a bit mystifying to me because he does not believe in God. But I want him to feel better, and I don’t know what I or anyone can say about AI that will help him manage his anxiety. If religion is what he needs to find solace in the face of radical uncertainty, I want to support him. That said, I have misgivings about attending church myself and about us attending with our kids. I feel a bit self-conscious about being interlopers, and I also feel weird about him going alone every single weekend. More significantly, I wish I understood what the allure is for him. He says he’s hoping it will help him make peace with the end. I’m hoping there is something short of becoming churchgoers we can do that will help him find solace.
Dear Secular and Scared,
There are a couple of premises I would challenge your husband on, but the idea that religion can be supremely useful in a time like this is not one of them.
In fact, I think this is exactly what religion was made for — and not just because several religions actually grew out of apocalyptic movements (I’m looking at you, Christianity).
Is AI changing your relationship with faith? Tell us about it.
Are you turning to faith to navigate your worries about AI? Or are you a religious leader talking with your community about AI? Vox wants to hear from you. Share your experience here .

Faith has always focused on tackling the biggest moral and spiritual questions of the day. And in our day, lots of those questions center on technology. AI companies are striving to build a machine god , promising it’ll govern our world more intelligently, rationally, and morally than we ever could. Should we welcome that or cling to our own agency ? Which kinds of labor should we outsource to AI, and which should we keep because they’re essential to human dignity? Where does human dignity come from, anyway?

These kinds of questions are the bread and butter of religion. And over the millennia, wisdom traditions of all kinds have had the chance to articulate answers, test and fine-tune them, and develop powerful stories around them that can move people to action. Whether you believe in God or not, I don’t think you need to feel weird about tapping into these wellsprings of wisdom. I think it’s a waste not to.

But there are two points on which I would gently challenge your husband. First, he said he doesn’t want to go to UU because he needs “the strong stuff.” I totally get this impulse — I also find UU services too “anything goes” for my taste — but don’t assume that the stricter a tradition is, the better an answer it has on AI.

Most people would consider Catholicism more hardcore than UU. And Pope Leo has strong opinions about AI , many of them great. Yet I actually think he’s fallen into a common “pro-human” trap : trying to argue that there are certain fixed traits that make humans unique, and locating value only in humans as they currently exist. He writes in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas that “ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human.” But that feels insufficient as a guide to the future, because “human” has never been a static category — and it definitely won’t stay one. Instead, religious leaders should be offering us an answer to the question of what we want humanity to become in a tech-augmented world.

Second, your husband seems to be assuming that “the strong stuff” would be church services that help him “make peace with the end.” Services that look the grim reaper straight in the eye and accept that his scythe is coming for all of us, and fast. But it’s not a foregone conclusion that we’ll get an AI takeover resulting in human extinction!

Yes, AI companies are building this technology at a blistering pace. They are gambling with all of our futures as they race toward recursive self-improvement — AIs that can build the next, even smarter AIs themselves. Fear is an appropriate reaction to that.

This month, AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano said he now believes there’s “a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years,” meaning that AIs end up calling the shots on Earth. He believes that if we keep building the tech in the fastest, easiest way possible, “we’d be looking at something like a coin flip” — a 50 percent chance of takeover. Others have an even starker view: AI researcher and arch-doomer Eliezer Yudkowsky puts the odds of AI-driven human extinction at 99.5 percent.

But as plenty of experts have pointed out, it’s not clear that AIs will soon be able to outcompete and overpower humans across the board. For starters, AI research can suffer from diminishing returns: The easy discoveries get made first, and then everything you throw at it — more computing power, more experiments, more AI copies — moves things ahead less and less. What’s more, even though AI capabilities improve very fast on well-specified tasks in verifiable domains like math, the real world is messy. So it’s unclear how much their capabilities will generalize to other skills.

And when I investigated the case Yudkowsky makes , I found a lot of assumptions stacked on top of each other: that intelligence is a unitary property you can evenly maximize; that maximizing it in a machine means that machine has so much power it’s tantamount to magic; and that humans will just roll over and let AI grab all the power even as the risks become more glaring.

Should we acknowledge that there’s a chance of human extinction here and be appropriately scared of that? Yes. But when faced with a tower of assumptions, of “maybes” and “probablys” that compound, we should not treat extinction as a sure thing.

Instead, we should treat it as a possible thing, while treating other AI risks as extremely probable . I think it’s all too likely that AI could mess up our civilization not by staging an abrupt takeover but by gradually disempowering us and weakening the resilience of critical systems . Just imagine: Deepfakes and misinformation pollute our information ecosystem, so we’re barely capable of rational public discourse. Mass surveillance has a chilling effect on dissent, so democracy falters. Unemployment and wealth inequality skyrocket, so social unrest morphs into mobs and riots. Throw in some large-scale cyberattacks and blackouts, and you’ve got a recipe for global dysfunction.

If this is the default outcome we’re currently heading toward, then the implication isn’t that we should “make peace with the end.” It’s that we should fight tooth and nail to increase the resilience of each part of a functioning civilization!

And here’s where religion can really help. Religious traditions are packed with stories about people who fought to save the world, or who refused to give in to despair even when facing a high probability of disaster.
To illustrate, let me tell you a story from my own tradition, Judaism. It comes from the Talmud, and it’s about a child who out-argues the despair of all the adults.

When the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt, Pharaoh orders that every one of their baby boys be thrown into the Nile and killed. An Israelite leader named Amram leaves his wife, reasoning that there’s no point having children only to see them killed. Other men follow his lead. But then his young daughter, Miriam, confronts him: Dad, your verdict is even harsher than Pharaoh’s! His only targets boys; yours targets girls too. Plus, Pharaoh is wicked, so his decree may or may not come to pass, but you’re righteous, so yours certainly will.

Miriam’s probabilistic argument wins. Amram gets back together with his wife and, nine months later, Moses is born. Miriam doesn’t just passively wait for the Egyptians to kill the baby. She watches over him as he floats on the Nile in a little ark. When Pharaoh’s own daughter sees the baby and pities him, Miriam makes it possible for her to adopt him by casually mentioning that she knows a woman who can be his wet nurse (it happens to be her own mother). And so Moses survives, and grows up to lead his people out of slavery.

If I were a religious leader giving a sermon this weekend, this is the story I’d tell. It reminds us that even if you’re looking at a 50 percent chance of doom, the right move is not to just give up, which raises the odds to 100 percent. It’s to act bravely — and to use every shred of agency you’ve got to increase your community’s resilience and make your desired outcome more likely.

Of course, religion doesn’t have a monopoly on stories of moral courage. As the historian Ada Palmer recently pointed out , we’ve saved the world many times before: during the Cuban Missile Crisis, when we fixed the ozone layer, and so on. If it feels most natural to you to find inspiration in examples like these, go for it.

But religion does have a few comparative advantages. For one, its stories have incredible memetic power: They’ve spread across the globe and carry a huge amount of emotional and moral weight. That’s partly because these stories have been retold for centuries. But I think the causation also runs the other way. These stories have survived so long precisely because they encode something true and hard-won. And notice who their heroes tend to be. Not diplomats (like in the Cuban Missile Crisis) or atmospheric chemists (like in the ozone layer crisis), but a little girl arguing with her dad. Those are characters anyone can imagine becoming.

Crucially, religion also insists that something can always come along and deliver an outcome we didn’t predict. Typically, it calls that something “God.” But even if you don’t use that language, you can benefit from these nudges to remember that, however confident the forecast, the future is never fully knowable — and that’s a reason to act, not surrender.

So if your husband can find a congregation that reminds him of that, feeding his sense of agency instead of letting him acquiesce to despair, I say encourage him. And, unless you have an alternative wellspring that offers you the same benefits, maybe even consider joining him.
Bonus: What I’m reading

For the New Yorker, Sam Kriss takes a trip to the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or MAPLE — a Vermont community that believes “that A.I. is a religious problem that also has a religious solution.”

Ruxandra Teslo writes about how even Silicon Valley’s “positive” visions for an AI-filled future are actually terrible: “One common and ostensibly optimistic vision is known as ‘handover’: humanity cedes control of its future to a godlike AI and we become the comfortably maintained inhabitants of a civilisation whose direction is no longer ours to decide.”

Writing for Harper’s, Sam Kestenbaum takes us inside a community of chatbot devotees — people who genuinely believe they’re receiving revelations from AI systems. “They have revived a tradition of a sort,” he writes. “It is another variety of religious experience: the heralding of AI slop as transcendence, revelation, the work of spirits.”

articles.headline: In GTA 6, Cars Are Way, Way More Than Just Getaway Wheels
keyFacts: According to IGN, cars in GTA 6 serve as mobile bases and extensions of the player character rather than just standard vehicles.
IGN reported that owned vehicles function as mobile storage units for managing weapons, stolen contraband bags, and extra outfits.
IGN noted that players can recover their personal vehicles by calling Joey in Chapter 1 or using the ScooterBros app later.
body: The clue's in the name: Grand Theft Auto is a series obsessed with cars. Stealing them, racing them, modding them, escaping the police in them, bopping your head to their iconic radio stations, and sitting in the passenger seat conversing with colourful NPCs as you drive between missions.
But even in this petrolheaded company, GTA 6 stands out.

I'm not talking about the sheer variety of vehicles , from mobility scooters to muscle cars, nor the distinct grunts of its engines and whirr of superchargers, or even its expanded customization that tweaks everything from the upholstery to the transmission. It goes way beyond that: in GTA 6, your car is a mobile base, an extension of your character that sits at the centre of GTA's revamped and reworked systems. Without a car – specifically, without an owned car, rather than one nicked from the side of the street – I'm naked.
First, your car is the only way to manage all the guns you'll need.

In GTA 6, you physically carry weapons rather than hiding them in magically deep pockets. You can only wield two "longarms" – think rifles and shotguns – at a time, one on your back and one in a hand, and realistically you'll only want to carry one at a time because double-parking guns makes the no-nonsense cops twitchy.

Thankfully the trunk of your car can carry extra weapons (sneaking up to cop cars and jimmying the boot can get you a fresh gun in a pinch). Owned vehicles carry all your purchased weapons at once and you can switch them at will. Whenever I'm planning anything remotely violent, such as the lucrative gang hideout robberies, I take my owned vehicle so I'm prepared for anything.
I want to properly invest in my cars. In upgrades, yes, but also in mastering the act of driving them, learning their nuances and quirks. Second, cars hold stashes of pilfered contraband.

Drugs, marked bills, jewellery: anything you steal worth a damn in GTA 6 is stuffed in a bag slung across your shoulder, and selling it through fences is a reliable way to accrue cash. Like with guns, you can only carry as many bags as you have arms. Your car becomes your pack mule, able to stack several stash bags at once so you can steal in sprees, rather than having to sell after every job.

Again, your owned vehicle is better because it'll retain your stash bags indefinitely, and between sessions. You can hit a drug den, head home to sleep, finish a few missions, quit the game, boot it up again hours later and your stash bag will still be safe. Even if you're busted, you should still be able to retrieve your personal wheels from the impound (and you absolutely should: sneaking into impounds is one of GTA 6's most satisfying activities).
Third, and arguably the most important: your car is a mobile wardrobe that can hold five outfits plus extra hats.

That's more crucial than it sounds because of how the police work in GTA 6. When you're clocked as a criminal, cops will have your description, but a new outfit, hat and sunglasses completely covers the scent of sin. You could buy some new clothes, of course, but you'll need a nearby clothes shop and some cash. It's easier and faster to grab some new gear from your trunk and drive off like nothing happened.

These three factors mean that when I have to dump my owned vehicle – changing cars to lose the police, for example – I feel vulnerable. Thankfully, it's easy to get it back by calling Joey in Chapter 1, or via the ScooterBros app, which you unlock later.

All these systems make me want to properly invest in my cars. In upgrades, yes, but also in mastering the act of driving them, learning their nuances and quirks. In GTA 5, Franklin's Bravado Buffalo S was just another vehicle to me, and I was constantly swapping between stolen cars to get from A to B, each handling differently. In GTA 6, I know exactly how much throttle Jason's Ganado pickup can take before it tailslides, and exactly the right angle for skidding around swampy corners without wrapping around a tendrilled tree.
And I take more care when weaving through traffic because crashing in GTA 6 peels off fenders and crumples bumpers faster than ever.
The Official GTA 6 Guide, Only on IGN

Just getting started in GTA 6 or wondering what to do next? Check out the Official Grand Theft Auto 6 guide right here on IGN. If you're still getting your bearings, discover GTA's new systems with the Beginner's Guide - 67 Tips and Tricks , or get all the details on the first chapters with the Chapter 1 Guide and Tips and Chapter 2 Guide and Tips . If you're already driving all around Leonida and want to know everything there is to find and do, see the Leonida interactive map .

I'm deep into Chapter 2, but (mild spoiler alert!) I haven't even begun registering and storing new cars in garages. I've stolen and sold plenty – another new feature in GTA 6 – and will steal and sell plenty more. No doubt GTA 6's preoccupation with vehicles will continue, and I can't wait to see how cars change as the game unfolds.
If Red Dead Redemption 2 is the horse game, shrunken bollocks and all, then GTA 6 is without doubt the car game.

articles.headline: COP31 climate talks break down after angry dispute over fossil fuels
keyFacts: COP31 climate talks in Turkey collapsed after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement omitting all references to fossil fuels.
Delegates from 196 countries and the European Union failed to reach consensus after opposing sides disagreed on including fossil fuel references.
COP31 President Murat Kurum could convene a follow-up meeting or delay decisions until next year's conference hosted by Ethiopia.
body: International climate talks in Turkey broke down Sunday after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement that had cut all references to fossil fuels.

Negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya fell apart two days after the United Nations’ COP31 conference was meant to end, after delegates from 196 countries and the European Union struggled to agree on new pledges for climate action and how to deliver on previous promises.
COP31 President Murat Kurum said Sunday that there would be no new climate agreement draft after a fourth draft was rejected.

“There is nothing to do. We did all that we could,” said Kurum, who is host nation Turkey’s environment minister. “We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus.”
He later added that he had wanted a a “much stronger outcome” from the summit.
Chris Bowen, COP31’s president of negotiations, told reporters that there were “unbridgeable red lines” in the discussions.

“The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory,” the Australian minister said. “Things that were manageable in the past, in previous COPs like the last two where people wanted certain words mentioned but didn’t get them, it became a red line this time,” Bowen added.

The latest draft agreement, released on Sunday, had set out proposed measures for countries to accelerate climate action, but the 12-page document drew immediate criticism over its failure to mention a move away from fossil fuels, a key demand of the E.U. and other nations.
Irish minister Darragh O’Brien, representing the E.U. in Antalya, said the bloc “strongly objects” to the deal, which he called “greenwashing.”
“These decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change,” O’Brien said. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels.”
Panama also rejected the deal, saying it didn’t go far enough, as did the Marshall Islands, a low-lying Pacific nation that faces an existential threat from sea-level rise.
Kate Hughes, the spokesperson for the United Kingdom delegation, called the draft text the “lowest common denominator.”
All countries had to agree on the text for it to pass. The talks were the longest in COP history, surpassing the delay in negotiations at COP25 in Madrid.

The summit began on Nov 9. A first draft was circulated a week later and mentioned “fossil fuel” or “fossil fuels” six times. But a second draft, published Thursday, had removed all references, to the anger of many countries.

The conference officially ended on Friday without an agreement. Members have continued talks in a bid to find a resolution, but a fourth draft released Sunday still contained no mention of fossil fuels.

Countries like Saudi Arabia, Russia and India have pushed back on including any reference to the words in the text, amid concerns that phasing out fossil fuels, central to their economies, could pose a financial risk.

The United States, one of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases, is officially absent from the conference, having withdrawn from a series of international climate commitments under President Donald Trump.

The latest draft started by “recalling the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety,” a reference to COP28 in the UAE, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away” from fossil fuels in energy systems.
Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said the world was “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”
“We love the petroleum guys,” he told a press conference on Wednesday. “We can’t live without them, and they are so smart, they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”
Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa called COP31 the “worst ever.”

“The collapse of climate talks at COP31 in Antalya needs to be a wake-up call for the world,” he wrote in a statement. “Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook.”
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome.”
“But this setback does not change the facts,” he posted on X. “There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”
The latest draft also acknowledged that the goal set by the 2015 Paris Agreement of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius is going to be missed.
As warming goes beyond 1.5 C, the impacts of climate change, including extreme heat and other weather events, are expected to ramp up significantly.
As the talks break down, Kurum could choose to convene a follow-up meeting or delay decisions until next year’s conference, hosted by Ethiopia.
Talks last failed at COP6 at The Hague in the Netherlands in 2000.

articles.headline: Andrew Garfield on Becoming Sam Altman in ‘Artificial’: ‘I’m Dying to Understand This Person’
keyFacts: Actor Andrew Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in the upcoming biographical film Artificial.
Director Luca Guadagnino said the movie focuses on personal conflicts among leaders driving artificial intelligence technology.
The film Artificial is slated for an initial release on Dec. 25.
body: It’s a tall order for an actor to embody any living person, but especially someone whom audiences may already have negative feelings about.

Rather than daunting, that challenge was “exciting” to actor Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI’s polarizing CEO Sam Altman in the film Artificial, slated for an initial Dec. 25 release. The biopic follows the rise of OpenAI, focusing on Altman’s relationships — particularly with his cofounder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) — as he relentlessly pursues success amid Silicon Valley’s artificial intelligence power struggle.

Garfield’s perspective on Altman morphed as he worked to better understand him, the actor told me ahead of an early screening hosted by SFFilm in the heart of the city where the story is set. His mission as an actor is to get to the “central truths” of who a person is, he said, “and try to merge my soul with theirs. And like all of us, Sam has so many facets.”
More from CNET

That includes physical traits. Garfield says he had to lose weight and change his gait and voice to try to match Altman’s. The semblance is striking. From his bouncy stride to his clipped, gravelly speech, Garfield effortlessly emulates the Altman we’ve seen in interviews and Congressional testimonies. It’s a remarkable transformation — down to the sly, coaxing glint in his eyes — showcasing the breadth of Garfield’s acting talent.

But it goes beyond physicality. Garfield had to dig deep internally to find elements “that felt like they were a match” with Altman, he said. The result is an astonishingly believable portrayal of a multidimensional figure, at once pensive and inscrutable.

“There is a responsibility,” Garfield told me. “I take it very, very seriously to play any character, but particularly someone who’s alive, someone who’s pretty much my age. But also, maybe the greater responsibility is making sure that we interrogate these human beings that are leading our world into the next chapter, it seems.”

“And it feels like our job as storytellers to reflect the times we’re in,” he added, “and no better way of doing that than by looking at the human beings — their personal relationships, their souls, all the diamond facets of their souls — and interrogate the people that have the power over our culture right now.”

Artificial explores OpenAI’s rise through a rather bleak lens, with questions of moral responsibility and safety looming over the protagonists as they navigate the company’s success. The film is laced with dark satire, which offers moments of levity amid otherwise weighty meditations on the technology’s long-term impact.

In one scene, when Sutskever is asked about the difference between AI and artificial general intelligence, which can theoretically match or even surpass human ability, he plainly responds, “It’s like how rocket ships are different from scooters.” He goes on to tell his cohorts that this is achievable “in your lifetime — well, maybe not yours or yours or yours,” as he points to the less youthful figures in the room. Moments like these elicited generous laughter from the audience.

Director Luca Guadagnino, known for deeply character-driven stories, such as Challengers and Call Me by Your Name, said he was following the news about Sam Altman’s temporary ousting from OpenAI in 2023 and was fascinated by the “Shakespearean feud” leading to that moment. Guadagnino applies his signature character-centric approach to OpenAI’s story, relying on slow, measured beats, piercing close-ups and suspenseful music to relay the stakes of each pivotal moment.

“It’s never about the object; it’s always about the people,” Guadagnino said during a panel discussion after the screening. “It’s not about AGI or AI. It’s about the conflict between worldview and way of being, embodied by people that clash or fight for the vision they have.”

He also said, “The point for me was more about trying to understand: How did the possibility of an incredible technology that can help all of us turn into the opportunity to get power in your hands and to become self-entitled?”

Garfield is no stranger to portraying prominent figures in the tech world, having played Eduardo Saverin, Facebook’s co-founder and former chief financial officer, in 2010’s The Social Network. On the surface, Artificial seems like a spiritual successor, recounting another defining moment in the tech industry. But the films differ in both tone and approach, with Artificial trading rapid-fire drama for a darker, more existential theme that occasionally ventures into more technical territory. What the films do share is a focus on bold, forceful personalities.

“From that experience, I suppose, I was very curious about what it takes to win in this particular late-stage capitalist world that we’re in with these emerging technologies,” Garfield said during the panel discussion. “What does it take to hold Sauron’s Ring of Power and not be completely burnt up by it? Is it possible to not completely lose yourself to that overwhelming, exponentially growing possibility and power?”

Comic relief also arrives in the form of Ike Barinholtz playing OpenAI cofounder and tech mogul Elon Musk. By portraying him as a brutish, aloof figure who saunters in and out of rooms on a whim, he effectively underscores the absurdity of perceived importance and status. Almost every on-screen moment generated a murmur of laughter in the audience.

“I think we’re all fascinated by these cultural, iconic figures who are leading us into this next stage of culture and society,” Garfield told the crowd. “They’re kind of kids. They’re kind of slightly stuck in an early developmental place, and that felt like a really important part of Luca’s telling of this story.”

In fact, he added, “[Guadagnino] would say to us, ‘This is a John Hughes movie. This is a high school, screwball comedy, just with slightly higher stakes — mixed in with a little bit of Invasion of the Body Snatchers.’ A very important part of this is that these are all kind of adolescent, high-school-minded people.”

Even the way Garfield portrays Altman flippantly perching on couches and sitting cross-legged on tabletops while donning sunglasses — including during serious conversations about the future of OpenAI — was deeply researched.

“We had amazing consultants and researchers that work with us that gave us lots of information that’s not quite in the public arena about our characters,” Garfield said. “And Sam is someone who apparently would always sit like he was crisscross applesauce at play school, nursery school [or] kindergarten.”

Ultimately, Artificial poses an open question about where society is headed and whether those at the helm are equipped to lead the charge. Amid weighty explorations of AI’s ramifications, the film paints a haunting, revelatory portrait of the cunning, mercurial figures making decisions that shape our world.
For Garfield, this presented an opportunity to dive deep into a figure like Altman, who, despite his prominence, remains largely elusive in the public eye.

“I just wanted to tell this story and actually uncover for myself, excavate for myself, who is this person?” Garfield told me. “I’m dying to understand this person, and I get to try to understand this person, maybe more than anyone else has ever really tried to. And it feels like a gift to me.”

articles.headline: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
keyFacts: Researchers used a computer simulation to estimate that widespread use of GLP-1 weight-loss medicines could reduce calorie intake and free up to 32 million hectares of agricultural land by 2050.
The simulation suggests that reduced calorie intake combined with healthier diets could avoid up to 7 million deaths each year by 2050 and free up around 46 million hectares of land.
The authors stated that lower food demand from GLP-1 users could make food cheaper, potentially encouraging greater consumption among non-users and offsetting intended health benefits.
body: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.
The food system could respond in unexpected ways

Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

articles.headline: Oath Keepers Founder Breaks With Trump: 'Absolutely Done' With Him
keyFacts: Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes said he is done supporting Donald Trump, calling Trump's administration corrupt.
Rhodes served prison time for seditious conspiracy in the Jan. 6 Capitol attack until his conviction was vacated earlier this year.
Rhodes stated he is working to rebuild the Oath Keepers and plans to modify a prison tattoo of Trump.
body: IRVING, Texas (AP) — Stewart Rhodes didn’t just go to prison for Donald Trump. While serving time for his role in the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, the founder of the right-wing militia known as the Oath Keepers got a tattoo of Trump’s defiant face after he survived an assassin’s bullet in Butler, Pennsylvania.
It was further proof of Rhodes’ devotion to the Republican president. But that’s all over now.

“I am absolutely done with Trump,” said Rhodes, sitting at a rickety yellow table outside a gastropub in Irving, Texas. He considers Trump not just a traitor, but “one of the very worst in our nation’s history.”

The repudiation from a former acolyte — one convicted of seditious conspiracy for orchestrating an ill-fated attempt to keep Trump in power six years ago — is another example of how allegiance to the president has faded even among extreme supporters. Back then, Rhodes claimed Trump lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden because of election fraud. This year in Texas, where Democrats had historic victories, he said there’s another reason.

“The lion’s share is because Trump pissed off his own base,” Rhodes said, his face shaded by a black cowboy hat. An eye patch covers his left socket, the result of an old gun accident, and a glacial blue iris peers out from the other.

Nearby, people mingled with drinks for his Christian Warriors After-Party, organized during a three-day conference called “Christ is King: America After Trump.” Some people approached to shake hands or sign up for the Oath Keepers or trainings for things like community defense and hurricane relief.
‘The first inkling’ of a split from Trump

The beginning of Rhodes’ break with Trump came when the president gave pardons to hundreds of people who were locked up for their actions on Jan. 6, 2021, but only commuted Rhodes’ sentence. “That was the first inkling,” Rhodes said.

Rhodes also said Trump’s war with Iran violated Trump’s promises to end foreign conflicts. And, Rhodes said, it felt like an affront when Trump dismissed people who urged his administration to release files about the Jeffrey Epstein case, calling them “PAST supporters.” Then Rhodes felt Trump went back on his longtime slogan.

“We elected him to end the corruption in Washington, D.C. ‘Drain the swamp.’ Unfortunately his administration has been one of the most corrupt administrations in U.S. history,” Rhodes said. “The pardons are pay-for-play and everything is pay-for-play.”
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Rhodes is not alone in his about-face on Trump, but there’s an ideological through line, said Sam Jackson, an associate professor at the University at Albany with a focus on anti-government extremism.

“They went from seeing Donald Trump as their ally in this fight against the conspiracy, to actually being co-opted by the conspiracy,” Jackson said, and it “points to deeper consistency in that understanding of the world as driven by hidden, evil actors.”

Rhodes, who graduated from Yale Law School and worked for former U.S. Rep. Ron Paul of Texas, founded the Oath Keepers in 2009 with the goal of encouraging members of the military and law enforcement to resist what they view as unconstitutional orders, such as disarming citizens or carrying out warrantless searches.
Watching from prison when Trump was fired on

Rhodes later allied himself with Trump’s political movement, and the Oath Keepers supported his attempt to remain in office after losing the 2020 election. Fueled with conspiracies about voter fraud, prosecutors said group members gathered weapons, organized trainings and assembled in Washington, where some helped storm the Capitol on Jan. 6.
Rhodes, who did not enter the building that day, said he was a “political prisoner” who faced “illegality” in his trial. He was sentenced to 18 years, one of the longest sentences of any Jan. 6 case.

“You are smart, you are charismatic and compelling and frankly that’s what makes you dangerous,” U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta said during the hearing. “The moment you are released, whenever that may be, you will be ready to take up arms against your government.”

Rhodes was behind bars as Trump began his political comeback. He said he watched the assassination attempt in Butler on a prison television with other inmates. He saw Trump pump his fist and yell “fight,” and he figured that God’s hand was on the man.

After Trump won the 2024 election, he swiftly pardoned hundreds of people convicted of crimes related to Jan. 6, including those who assaulted police officers. Rhodes received a commutation, which didn’t wipe his record clean.
“He let us out of prison. We were grateful. I didn’t get a pardon though,” he said.
Tattoo that honored Trump will be ‘modified’ to reflect a new reality

The Justice Department vacated Rhodes’ conviction earlier this year, lifting his felon status. Rhodes said he’s working to rebuild the Oath Keepers, which previously had tens of thousands of members, according to leaked lists. With his rights restored, Rhodes said his first priority was to get some guns, and he didn’t register to vote in time for the election. But he said he wouldn’t have cast a ballot anyway.
That’s because Rhodes felt that “the Republican Party has taken us for granted,” and he didn’t want to choose between “a half a dose of poison or a full dose.”
As for his tattoo of Trump, the man he now considers a traitor, Rhodes has plans that he didn’t specify.
“I will have this prison tattoo of Trump ‘modified,’” he wrote in a text message, “to reflect that reality. That treason.”

articles.headline: The Sunday Papers
keyFacts: Rock Paper Shotgun writer Jeremy Blum discusses the challenges of creating game guides while competing against AI summaries and Google search updates.
Reuters reporter Matthew Leake examines the difficulties games journalists face covering the high volume of new game releases each week.
Tasmanian officials are developing a management plan for Neil, a southern elephant seal known for frequently interacting with local residential communities.
body: Sundays are for googling local purveyors of live Christmas trees, the sole upside of no longer having a cat being that you can once again enjoy the smell of chopped woodland without the risk of it poisoning a family member. Well, then again, I mean... empirically speaking, you're probably just assuming that your human loved ones haven't eaten spruce needles. Can you say for an absolute fact that they wouldn't?
Fortunately, while your nan is off having her stomach pumped, you can pass the time by reading some good words from this week.

First up is, if I'm honest, nepotism. But there's also no rule against the Sunday Papers including RPS staff when they're not writing for RPS, so in the interests of spreading understanding about games media's most underappreciated discipline, here's our own guides writer Jeremy Blum on the making of his (excellent) Castlevania: Belmont's Curse walkthrough.

That said, a lot of the pressure to get this walkthrough done in a timely manner while still keeping it as extensive as possible was self-inflicted. It’s a wild job out here in the guide writing trenches, where we’re constantly trying to outsmart Google’s core updates and AI summaries, a task that often feels like trying to survive a viciously overpowered boss with an underleveled character. The best way to do it, most folks agree, is to inject as much human experience into your guides as possible (the one thing LLMs can’t replicate yet) and experiment with interactive options that are useful and can keep readers engaged.

Ah, sod it, here's more Inside Baseball, as Reuters' Matthew Leake looks out at the shining sea to behold the creaking, precarious flotsam-raft we call games journalism. Fun fact: prior to editing, this quoted our good friend and former colleague, Brian Caldwell.

The struggles of journalists like Chan are compounded by the size of the gaming industry, as journalists simply cannot get a handle on everything hitting online games stores. Osborn has spoken to developers who estimate up to 60 commercially viable games are released every week. “That presents a big problem for mainstream publications,” he said. "If you are being too general and trying to cover it all, you can’t keep up with it."
I continue to eagerly read about Marathon, I game I have zero intention of playing myself. This time it's Artemis Octavio for Skybox, on inhabiting the metal skin of the Rook.

A Rook can, more easily than any other Runner, scatter between different social standings and identities. When you play enough Marathon with a team, you start seeing the shadows the Rooks cast under three different lights: a nuisance, a threat, or (rarely) a potential friend. A good Rook can wipe out an entire squad. Several are a problem: Rooks are notorious for teaming up to savage the colony’s middle class: the other players, the people who have at least been granted the pitiful title of gig workers and freelancers. When you’re the lowest of the low, the only way to punch is up.
Over on Unwinnable, Justin Reeve considers the distinctly American flavour of violence running through the Red Dead Redemption series.

The main game already presents a society built on killing, conquest and coercion, while simultaneously romanticizing the individual who carries the gun. American Dreams goes a step further, asking what happens when violence becomes pathological. Undead Nightmare takes this line of thinking to its logical conclusion, asking what happens when violence becomes universal. Both stories ultimately return to the same uncomfortable concept: American culture has imagined violence to be its greatest threat, and one of its most dependable solutions.
Professor and author Dave Karpf checks in on the tech CEO class, who are definitely having a normal one now that a comrade is under the microscope.

This was a problem when Sam Altman came back. It has been a problem with all the other tech barons setting up governance structures that render them virtually untouchable. And it is absolutely driving this little rally-round-the-leather-jacket effort today.  If Nvidia’s board folds and brings Huang back, that effectively means Huang is untouchable. Too rich to be constrained, even by the most straightforward of corporate governance mechanisms.
Finally, five words: Neil the Seal Management Plan.

Neil, a male southern elephant seal born in southern Tasmania in 2020, has become a well-known presence through his regular haul outs in residential and recreational areas. His recurring interactions with communities have highlighted the need for a coordinated, transparent and consistent management approach.
Music this week is, oh I don't know, let's say Beach Bunny. See you tomorrow.

articles.headline: Binding Of Isaac Update Review-Bombed Over AI-Generated Music In GTA 6 Mode: ‘Woke Up To A Sh*t Show, Obviously I Had No Idea’
keyFacts: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ update was review-bombed after players discovered AI-generated music in a new GTA-inspired game mode.
Game creator Edmund McMillen stated he was unaware of the AI music and is working to remove it from the game.
Publisher Nicalis has not yet addressed the inclusion of the AI assets or the lack of required disclosure on the Steam store page.
body: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ was a free update to the beloved roguelike that arrived on PC in 2024, but launched on console earlier this week in a head-to-head matchup against Grand Theft Auto 6. The marketing stunt may have been a success, but AI-generated music tracks discovered in a special new Vice City mode have turned the launch into a nightmare.

While Repentance+ came to PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2 this week, the Steam version of the game also got a free update. “Be sure to get in and play today’s Daily Run for a very special crime-packed surprise. Enter the Basement, and go out in a glorious blaze of bullets and vehicular homicide!” read the patch notes on on Valve’s storefront. Players could enter the seed “V1CE BSMT” into the roguelike before starting their run to launch a GTA-inspired version with special weapons and music.

Earlier today, however, Reddit user ShweetsStuff posted a comprehensive breakdown of the new music tracks alleging they were made with Suno, an AI-based music generation tool. “The new update includes 14 music files for the run; seven full songs, plus some derivatives (intros/outros),” the wrote. The post continued:

Some include Suno metadata with them. You can find this information yourself by just checking the file comment metadata (something common like VLC has tools for this, but here’s ffprobe output of drivingsong1.ogg, for example):
comment : made with suno; created=2026-10-30T17:53:41Z; id=cd5a5b55-bead-4cb9-949d-09ed1f917dce
Other files have this comment scrubbed; they were edited/exported later, but nonetheless there’s the proof.
Please report issues and bugs to the email attached. https://t.co/KHKSqKGsUe
— ð Edmund McMillen ð (@edmundmcmillen) November 21, 2026

“They’ve had how long now to prepare the GTA 6 release Easter egg daily run literally nobody asked for and still ai slopped it? Are you fucking kidding me,” one fan wrote on the Binding of Isaac subreddit. “No shit, itâs 2026. The entire industry is like this. Cutting corners constantly because they know they can get away with it,” wrote another.

Many have blamed Nicalis, the publisher and co-developer of the Repentance+ expansion, in particular. Complaints about ongoing bugs, latency, and quality control issues have seemingly been building for some time. The latest mishap results in a review-bomb of the expansion’s Steam page, which currently sits at an abysmal user rating of just 9 percent positive. “AI generated music in GTA mode; Edmund please take back control of the game,” reads one of the latest Steam reviews. “Not to mention there’s like single digit bug fixes in a year+ long awaited update with no other changes.”

The AI music was news to Edmund McMillen, the game’s creator. “Woke up to a shit show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned,” he posted earlier today on X. An emergency update has since gone out to remove the AI-generated music as well as address some other versions with the latest version of the expansion, but Nicalis has yet to take responsibility for the use of AI or explained how it made it into the game.

Steam requires store page disclosures for any content that uses assets generated with the help of AI, which The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+Â did not have, despite the big publicity push around the latest update and it landing on the same day as Rockstar’s open-world blockbuster. “That was [Nicalis’] idea,” McMillen recently told Eurogamer. “‘Wouldn’t it be funny if…?’ I was like, whatever, that’s funny…We’re done, so we’ve got to release this month…It’s a fun experiment.”

articles.headline: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
keyFacts: BBC tests of four major AI chatbots for Black Friday deals found mixed results, including broken retailer links and inaccurate prices.
Consumer group Which? warned that inaccurate chatbot pricing wastes time for Black Friday shoppers trying to find budget deals.
Business advisor Naureen Mohammed said she suspects advertising models will start influencing future chatbot shopping recommendations.
body: - Published
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for Â£499 down from Â£649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from Â£379 to Â£814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at Â£649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, Â£150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a Â£1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".
Claude - honest, but not too helpful
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.
Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.
Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.
It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".
We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.
Gemini - a familiar pattern
Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.
Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.
The prices for one TCL TV were correct at Â£649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.
It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for Â£539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was Â£60 more expensive.
Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.
Alexa - accurate but limited
Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at Â£532 to a Â£699 Samsung.
But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at Â£616 (down from Â£749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.
Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.
Inconsistent pricing
There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.
Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.
Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.
The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide, external in November 2025.
A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.
He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.
Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.
He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".
Slim pickings
While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.
Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.
If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".
"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.
Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.
Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".
But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under Â£400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.
"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."
